headline: Chimpanzees throw stones at the same trees for years

sources.title: Chimpanzees have been hurling rocks at the same trees for more than a decade (ScienceDaily)
Why Do Male Chimpanzees Throw Rocks At the Same Trees for More Than a Decade? (AllAfrica, republishing The Conversation)
Chimpanzees Keep Throwing Stones at the Same Trees, Scientists Want To Know Why (SciTechDaily)

chunks.text: Male chimpanzees in West Africa have been throwing stones at the same trees for years, scientists say. The [[habit]] was reported in late August 2026 from a national park in the region, a savanna-woodland [[landscape]]. The males {{pick up}} stones and throw them at [[particular]] trees. They {{come back to}} the same spots, so [[piles]] of rocks have {{built up}} at the base. The throwing sites have been [[in active use]] for more than ten years.

verbs.correct: To lift something from the ground
verbs.why: Kids pick up shells on the beach, and a gardener picks up fallen branches after a storm. Here the male chimps pick up stones from the ground and throw them at particular trees.

verbs.correct: To return to the same place
verbs.why: Birds come back to the same nest every spring, and families come back to a favorite campsite each summer. These chimps come back to the same spots again and again, year after year.
Dust builds up on a shelf nobody cleans, and snow builds up against a door overnight. Because the chimps keep throwing, piles of rocks have built up at the base of those trees.

chunks.text: The behavior {{stands out}} because it is so rare: only four chimpanzee groups in West Africa have been [[observed]] doing it. Researchers from the University of Victoria and local [[field assistants]] {{set out}} to learn why. The chimps are unhabituated, not used to humans, so the team could not watch them directly. Instead, they {{set up}} [[camera traps]] and audio recorders at the sites, scanned the rocks in 3D, and measured the trees. They also noted [[nests]] and [[feeding signs]] and slowly {{put together}} a picture of the behavior.

verbs.correct: To be clearly different from others
verbs.wrong: To represent an idea or a group
verbs.why: A red coat stands out in a gray crowd, and one tall building stands out on a flat skyline. This behavior stands out because it has only been observed in four chimpanzee groups in all of West Africa.

verbs.correct: To begin a task with a clear goal
verbs.wrong: To keep something for later use
verbs.why: A hiker sets out to reach the top before noon, and a detective sets out to find the missing money. The research team set out to learn why the chimps throw stones at these trees.

verbs.correct: To put equipment in place for use
verbs.wrong: To make an alarm or camera start
verbs.why: Campers set up a tent before dark, and a band sets up its speakers before a show. Since the chimps are not used to humans, the team set up camera traps and audio recorders at the sites instead of watching in person.

verbs.correct: To create something from many parts
verbs.why: A child puts together a puzzle piece by piece, and a reporter puts together a story from many small facts. The researchers put together a picture of the chimps' behavior from cameras, recordings, scans, and measurements.

chunks.text: The researchers have not {{figured out}} why. The throwing is part of a bigger [[display]]: the males also call loudly and drum on the tree's buttress roots. It may be a [[tradition]] {{passed down}} in these groups, or serve a symbolic [[purpose]], such as marking [[territory]]. Or the males may be {{showing off}} their [[status]]. The team cannot {{rule out}} any of these ideas, so the reason remains [[an open question]]. It is a rare case of stone use that is purely social, not to [[crack]] nuts or get food.

verbs.correct: To find the answer to a question
verbs.wrong: To watch for signs of danger
verbs.why: A mechanic figures out why a car will not start, and a student figures out a hard math problem. The researchers still have not figured out why the chimps throw stones at all.

verbs.correct: To teach a habit to the next generation
verbs.wrong: To choose not to include someone
verbs.why: A recipe is passed down from grandmother to grandchild, and old songs are passed down in a village for centuries. One theory is that the stone throwing is a tradition passed down within these particular chimp communities.

verbs.correct: To display skill to impress others
verbs.wrong: To arrive at a place at a set time
verbs.why: A skater shows off a new trick in front of his friends, and a cook shows off her knife skills behind the counter. Another idea is that the males are showing off their skill or status to other chimps.

verbs.correct: To decide that something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To test an idea with an experiment
verbs.why: A doctor rules out a broken bone after an X-ray, and a weather report cannot rule out rain. The researchers cannot rule out any of their three ideas about why the chimps do this.

chunks.text: For now, the chimps {{carry on}} with their stone throwing, and the researchers plan to keep studying the sites. But their [[habitat]] is not secure. The area is [[under threat]] from bauxite [[mining]] exploration. If mining begins, it could {{push the chimps out}} of the landscape they have used for so long. The team hopes this rare behavior will help people see why these forests are worth protecting.

verbs.wrong: To do a planned piece of work
verbs.why: Workers carry on after a short break, and a teacher carries on with the lesson after the bell. For now, the chimps carry on with their stone throwing while the researchers keep studying the sites.

verbs.correct: To force someone to leave a place
verbs.wrong: To ask strongly for a change
verbs.why: High rents push families out of a city, and a new road can push deer out of a valley. If bauxite mining begins, it could push the chimps out of the landscape they have used for so long.

mainIdea.s: Male chimps in West Africa have thrown stones at the same trees for over ten years. Scientists studied the sites indirectly and still do not know why the chimps do it.
mainIdea.why: The same throwing sites have been in active use for more than ten years, the team studied them with camera traps and recorders, and the reason is still an open question.

mainIdea.s: Researchers in West Africa proved that male chimps throw rocks at trees to mark their territory. Camera traps at the sites recorded the behavior for more than a decade.
mainIdea.why: Close, but marking territory is only one of several theories. The researchers say they cannot rule out any of the ideas yet.

mainIdea.s: A new study found that chimps in a national park in West Africa crack nuts with stone hammers. The scientists say young animals learn the skill by watching their mothers.
mainIdea.why: These chimps use stones in a purely social way, not to crack nuts or get food. Nothing in the study is about young animals learning from their mothers.

tf.s: Scientists now know why the chimps throw the stones.
tf.why: Marking territory is only one theory. The researchers have not figured out why the chimps do it, and they cannot rule out any of the ideas yet.

tf.s: The team set up camera traps at the throwing sites.
tf.why: They also placed audio recorders, made 3D scans of the rocks, and measured the target trees.

tf.s: Stone throwing is common among chimps across Africa.
tf.why: The behavior stands out because it is so rare. It has been seen in only four chimp groups in West Africa.

tf.s: Mining could push the chimps out of the area.
tf.why: The area is under threat from bauxite mining exploration, and if mining begins it could push the chimps out of the landscape they have used for so long.

tf.s: The chimps are used to having people nearby.
tf.why: They are unhabituated, so the team set up cameras and recorders at the sites instead of watching the chimps directly.

tf.s: Piles of rocks have built up under the target trees.
tf.why: The chimps come back to the same spots again and again, and the sites have been in use for more than ten years.

lines.text: Did you see the story about the chimps in West Africa? The males {{pick up}} stones and throw them at the same trees, and they've been doing it for more than ten years.
The same trees, for ten years? [[Talk about a habit]].
Yes. They {{come back to}} the same spots, so big piles of rocks have {{built up}} under the trees.
That is strange, though. [[What on earth for]]?
[[Your guess is as good as mine]]. The scientists couldn't watch the chimps directly, so they {{set up}} camera traps and audio recorders and slowly {{put together}} a picture of what was happening.
And they still haven't {{figured out}} why?
Not yet. One idea is that it's a tradition {{passed down}} in the group. Another is that the males are {{showing off}}. They can't {{rule out}} anything.
The showing off idea sounds right to me. [[Boys will be boys]]. Don't they drum on the trees and make loud calls at the same time?
Right, and it {{stands out}} because only four groups in West Africa do it.
I read that the area is being explored for mining. Could the chimps still {{carry on}} with it if that happens?
Maybe not. [[Fingers crossed]] the forest gets protected before it comes to that.

expressions.def: "Talk about" plus a noun is used to say something is an extreme example of that thing
ex: Three hours stuck in traffic. Talk about a bad day.
He checks his phone every minute. Talk about a habit.

expressions.def: A stronger way to ask "why?" when something seems to make no sense
ex: You bought a second fridge? What on earth for?
She's learning Latin. What on earth for?

expressions.expr: Your guess is as good as mine
expressions.def: Used to say that you do not know the answer either
ex: When will the bus come? Your guess is as good as mine.
Why did he quit? Your guess is as good as mine.

expressions.def: Used, often as a joke, to say that loud or show-off behavior from males is normal and expected
ex: They spent the whole party arm wrestling. Boys will be boys.
My brothers still race each other to the car. Boys will be boys.

expressions.def: Used to say you hope something good will happen
ex: Fingers crossed the weather stays dry for the wedding.
I sent the application this morning. Fingers crossed.
